summary: Documents the process then used to standardize Internet protocols and procedures. It was replaced by RFC 1602, and the process has been revised since.

plainLanguage.summary: The rule book for how an idea becomes an official Internet standard: who looks at it, how long it waits, and what steps it must pass.

questions: what is the internet standards process
how does a protocol become a standard
what is the difference between proposed standard and draft standard
who decides if something becomes an internet standard
subtitle: How Internet protocols evolve from proposals to official standards.

tldr.problem: The Internet needs a rigorous way to develop and approve protocols and standards so that different vendors and engineers can build compatible systems that work together globally.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a formal multi-stage process where protocol proposals move through maturity levels (Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, Standard) with community review, implementation, and operational testing at each stage, overseen by the Internet Activities Board (IAB) and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).
tldr.outcome: The process has evolved since 1992 and remains the framework for Internet standardization, though it has been updated multiple times. It has produced a reliable foundation for Internet protocol development.

today: RFC 1310 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1602. The standards process itself has continued to evolve through updates including RFC 2026 (Proposed Standard for the Standards Track) and beyond. The core principle of requiring implementation experience and community consensus before standardization remains central to how the Internet develops protocols today.

sections.title: Why Standards Matter
sections.content:
The Internet connects millions of independent networks and systems. For them all to communicate, they must follow the same protocols—agreements about how to send and receive data. Internet Standards are specifications that are stable, well-understood, technically competent, have multiple independent implementations, and are demonstrably useful. Without a formal process for creating them, the Internet would fracture into incompatible pieces.

This RFC documents the process used by the Internet community to create, test, and approve standards. The process evolved over three years of practical experience and aims to achieve four goals: high quality, prior implementation and testing, openness and fairness, and timeliness.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if every company built cars differently and they could not drive on the same roads. A standards process is like rules that let everyone build compatible cars.

sections.title: The Organizations and Their Roles
sections.content:
The Internet Activities Board (IAB) is the primary coordinating committee for Internet design and engineering. It has delegated most standardization work to the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). The IETF is organized into Working Groups focused on specific technical areas, each led by an Area Director. Final decisions on standards are made by the IAB based on recommendations from the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), which is made up of Area Directors and the IETF Chair.

The IETF's spirit of cooperation is crucial: participation is by individual technical contributors rather than formal organizational representatives. The process works because participants prioritize creating technically superior protocols that benefit the entire Internet community.

The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) manages the assignment of protocol parameters like port numbers, version numbers, and MIB numbers. These must be coordinated to avoid conflicts.
sections.plainLanguage: Different groups of engineers focus on different parts of the Internet. They discuss ideas, vote on which ones are good, and the top group (the IAB) makes the final decision.

sections.title: Types of Specifications and Tracks
sections.content:
Specifications come in two main types: Technical Specifications (which describe a protocol, format, or procedure) and Applicability Statements (which define when and how Technical Specifications should be used). Applicability Statements can specify requirement levels: Required (must be implemented), Recommended (should be implemented), or Elective (optional).

Standards-track specifications follow a three-stage maturity model. Proposed Standard is the entry level: the specification is stable and has received community review, though implementation and testing are optional. Draft Standard requires at least two independent, interoperable implementations and operational experience. Standard requires significant implementation experience and operational deployment. Importantly, a specification must spend at least 6 months at Proposed Standard and 4 months at Draft Standard before advancing.

Specifications that do not fit the standards track are published with different labels: Experimental (for ideas being tested), Informational (for reference documents not representing consensus), and Historic (for old specifications that have been superseded or deprecated).
sections.plainLanguage: Ideas go through three levels: maybe it will work, probably it will work, definitely it works. At each level, engineers test it more before moving it forward.

sections.title: How an Idea Becomes a Standard
sections.content:
A protocol specification can originate from an IETF Working Group, an individual engineer, or an external organization. The key steps are:

  • Internet Draft phase: The working document is shared in the IETF Internet Drafts directory and stays there for at least two weeks, allowing wide community comment. Drafts are temporary and automatically removed after six months without IESG recommendation.
  • Working Group review: The document is refined based on feedback and discussion in open meetings and mailing lists.
  • IESG evaluation: When a document is ready, the responsible Working Group asks its Area Director to submit it to the IESG. The IESG determines if independent technical review is needed and whether the specification meets the criteria for its maturity level.
  • IAB approval: The IESG sends its recommendation to the IAB for final approval. The IAB communicates the decision back to the IETF and asks the RFC Editor to publish it.
  • Advancement: Specifications can advance to higher maturity levels when they meet the criteria (implementation experience, operational use, community consensus).
sections.plainLanguage: An engineer writes a draft, shows it to other engineers who test it and give feedback, and if everyone agrees it works, it gets approved and published officially.

sections.title: Requirement Levels and Applicability
sections.content:
Internet Standards use RFC 2119 requirement levels to clarify what implementations must do. A Required feature must be implemented for conformance (e.g., all TCP/IP systems must implement IP and ICMP). A Recommended feature should be included unless there is a special reason to omit it. An Elective feature is optional for implementation.

For specifications not on the standards track, two additional requirement levels exist: Limited Use (appropriate only in special circumstances, such as experimental protocols) and Not Recommended (inappropriate for general use).

An external specification from organizations like ISO or CCITT can be incorporated by reference into an Internet Standard, but the Internet community will not standardize a competing "Internet version" unless there is an explicit cooperative agreement. Similarly, vendor specifications that become de facto standards can be adopted formally through a documented process.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules say whether something MUST be done, SHOULD be done, or MAY be done. This way engineers know what is truly required versus what is just suggested.

sections.title: Status and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 1310 itself is Informational, not a Standard, and has been obsoleted by RFC 1602. The Internet standards process documented here was revised multiple times as the IETF and Internet grew. RFC 1602 provided an update in 1994, and the process has continued to evolve with subsequent RFCs (such as RFC 2026).

The fundamental approach has remained sound: iterative development with community input, implementation and testing before standardization, and careful governance through the IETF and IAB. This process has produced Internet Standards that have successfully guided decades of Internet protocol development and evolution.
sections.plainLanguage: This rule book was updated as the Internet grew and people learned what worked best. The core idea of testing before standardizing is still used today.
